hypotheses.reasoning: At 19:58:49 the redis node was swapped out and came back with 0 keys and no RDB snapshot (#1023). Before that, redis stats showed a normal hit rate. About a minute later order-service reported a 96% miss ratio (baseline 2%) and fell back to postgres for every read (#1089). That stampede pushed postgres to 490/500 connections and 95-96% CPU (#1107, #1159). Simple lookups by id slowed to 5-9s (#1090, #1428), order-service queries hit their 5s timeout (#1236, #1473), and the gateway returned 504s on /checkout (#1173 onward). The trigger, a cold cache, would have been survivable alone. The damage came from every cache miss going to the database at once, which is a cache stampede. The status-poller errors against a deprecated legacy-inventory endpoint started at 19:54, before the onset, and are not on the checkout path, so I treated them as a red herring. I found no deploy lines.
Postgres connection slots and CPU were near their limits. But this happened because of the cache-miss flood, not on its own.
Order-service queries to postgres timed out. That is the direct failure mode, but it was driven by the cold cache.

verdict.recommendedAction: Warm the redis cache for hot order keys, or use request coalescing or single-flight on cache misses. Throttle postgres fallback reads until the hit ratio recovers. Turn on RDB/AOF persistence or warm-up for redis so a replaced node doesn't start empty. Separately, remove the status-poller check against the deprecated legacy-inventory endpoint.
